claim: The statutory federal tax lien arises by operation of law when three things have happened: the tax is assessed, notice and demand for payment is made, and the taxpayer neglects or refuses to pay. IRC 6321: 'If any person liable to pay any tax neglects or refuses to pay the same after demand, the amount (including any interest, additional amount, addition to tax, or assessable penalty, together with any costs that may accrue in addition thereto) shall be a lien in favor of the United States upon all property and rights to property, whether real or personal, belonging to such person.' IRC 6322: the lien 'shall arise at the time the assessment is made and shall continue until the liability ... is satisfied or becomes unenforceable by reason of lapse of time.' So once the taxpayer fails to pay after demand, the lien dates back to the assessment date. IRC 6303 requires the notice and demand 'as soon as practicable, and within 60 days, after the making of an assessment'. IRC 6321 sets no fixed number of days between demand and the lien. The '10 days after notice and demand' in IRM 5.19.4.2 is a precondition for levy, not for the lien.
sourceDate: IRM 5.12.1 effective 07-11-2018; IRC text read on Cornell LII; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IRM 5.12.1.3: 'The following must occur for the "statutory" lien to arise: An assessment must have been made; Notice and demand for payment must have been made; and The taxpayer must have neglected or refused to pay.' IRS 'Understanding a federal tax lien' (https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/understanding-a-federal-tax-lien, last reviewed 14-Sep-2026) lists the same three steps. The texts of IRC 6321, 6322 and 6303 come from https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6321, /6322 and /6303.
uncertainty: The statute text was read on Cornell LII, which is a secondary host. uscode.house.gov and govinfo did not return readable text to the fetch. No source states a minimum number of days that must pass after the demand before payment counts as neglected. graceDaysBeforeLienArises is null: NOT FOUND, and the statute names no such period.
designImplication: Model the statutory lien as attaching on the first unpaid bill (the notice and demand), dated back to the assessment date. It is private until an NFTL is filed. Keep 'lien exists' and 'NFTL filed' as separate states.

claim: Revenue officer (field) guideline: 'In general, an NFTL should be filed' when 'the aggregate UBA is $10,000 or more' (UBA means the total unpaid assessed balance across all periods). It should also be filed when an installment agreement does not meet the streamlined, guaranteed or in-business trust fund express criteria, and when an open account with UBA of $10,000 or more is reported currently not collectible. Below $10,000: 'Generally NFTLs will not be filed when the UBA is less than $10,000, but they may be filed if they will protect the government's interest, such as in the case of an impending bankruptcy or other exigent circumstances.' A floor applies below that: 'Except in rare circumstances, an NFTL should not be filed when the balance to be reflected on the NFTL is less than $2,500.' ACS (phone and letter collection) uses the same $10,000 line. IRM 5.19.4.5.3.2 says to file for non-exempt installment agreements, currently-not-collectible closures, queue reassignments and continuous wage levies 'when the aggregate assessed balance is $10,000 or more'. 'Managerial approval is required when a decision to file a NFTL on an account where the aggregate assessed balance is less than $10,000 has been made.' Filing is a determination, not automatic. A revenue officer makes it within 10 calendar days of the first contact or attempted contact (IRM 5.12.2.3.2).

value.belowThresholdAllowedIf: protect government interest (e.g. bankruptcy, dissipating assets); manager approval in ACS

establishes: IRM 5.12.2.6 table ('the aggregate UBA is $10,000 or more / file an NFTL') and its Notes on $10,000 and $2,500. IRM 5.19.4.5.3.2 and 5.19.4.5.3.4 (https://www.irs.gov/irm/part5/irm_05-019-004r) for ACS. Pub 594 (Rev. 1-2026) says that by law no NFTL is filed for an ACA individual shared responsibility payment.
uncertainty: The $10,000 is an internal guideline, not a statute. The IRS may file at any balance once the lien exists. Whether the $10,000 includes accrued, unassessed interest and penalty: the IRM says UBA is assessed balance only, so it does not. IRM 5.12.2 still uses the word 'streamlined', which IRM 5.14.5 (07-21-2026) has renamed 'Simple Payment Plan'.
designImplication: Gate NFTL filing on assessed balance >= $10,000, with a $2,500 floor below which it almost never happens. Treat filing as a probabilistic or discretionary event above the line, not a certainty on a fixed day. Accrued, unassessed interest does not count toward the line.

claim: An NFTL determination is not required for the plans the IRS approves without a financial statement. As of 2026 these are: a Simple Payment Plan (formerly the Streamlined Installment Agreement), available when 'the aggregate unpaid balance of assessment ... is $50,000 or less', and a Guaranteed IA under IRC 6159(c), available when income tax owed is $10,000 or less excluding penalties and interest, with full payment within 3 years. IRM 5.14.5.2: 'A Notice of Federal Tax Lien (NFTL) determination is not required when granting a Simple Payment Plan. However, revenue officers (ROs) may file an NFTL at their discretion when they determine filing is appropriate to protect the government's interest', which requires documented justification and manager concurrence. The July 2026 IRM 'Removed the prior two-tier $25,000/$25,001-$50,000 structure and 72-month minimum payment rule'. Plans of $25,000 or less and plans above $25,000 now differ only in their agreement locator code (XX36 vs XX37). Above $50,000, or for a plan needing a financial statement, an NFTL determination must be made (IRM 5.14.1.4.3). In ACS, a non-exempt IA with an aggregate assessed balance of $10,000 or more and a required financial statement means 'file NFTL'. NFTLs 'may be filed: While IAs are pending; In connection with granting IAs; During the rejection process; During the default/termination period'. Filing while an IA is in effect is 'not general practice' and needs group manager approval and exigent circumstances. ACS: a continuous wage levy with UBA under $25,000 that pays in 60 months or less needs no NFTL determination.

value.fileWhileIAInEffect: only with group manager approval and exigent circumstances

sourceDate: IRM 5.14.5 effective 07-21-2026; IRM 5.14.1 effective 07-20-2026; IRM 5.12.2 effective 07-12-2024; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IRM 5.14.5.2 (Simple Payment Plans, $50,000 or less, NFTL determination not required) and 5.14.5.3 (Guaranteed IA, 'An NFTL determination is not required for a guaranteed IA; however, an NFTL may be filed at the discretion of the revenue officer'). IRM 5.12.2.3.1: 'An NFTL filing determination is not required on Guaranteed/Streamlined Installment Agreements or In-Business Trust Fund Express Agreements.' IRM 5.14.1.4.3 (https://www.irs.gov/irm/part5/irm_05-014-001r). IRM 5.19.4.5.3.2 (ACS). Pub 594 (Rev. 1-2026), on any approved plan: 'we will still charge applicable interest and penalties ... and may file a Notice of Federal Tax Lien'.
uncertainty: IRM 5.14.5 is written for field revenue officers. ACS's IRM 5.19.4 (12-30-2024) still says 'streamlined' and has not been read as updated to the $50,000 Simple Payment Plan wording. The older $25,000 'no lien' streamlined threshold, which secondary sources still repeat, is superseded in the field IRM. Whether ACS applies $25,000 or $50,000 as the no-determination line for individual IAs today is not stated in one current ACS paragraph. ACS treats an IMF streamlined IA as needing no financial statement, so 'an NFTL is not required'. No source says an NFTL can never be filed for a plan of $50,000 or less; it is discretionary.
designImplication: An individual who sets up a payment plan with assessed balance <= $50,000 should normally avoid an NFTL. Above $50,000, or after a default, an NFTL is the expected result once the balance is >= $10,000. The $25,000 line now matters for lien withdrawal (DDIA), not for filing.

claim: No single notice in the CP501/CP503/CP504/LT11 sequence triggers filing. What the IRS requires is a written warning of possible NFTL filing on each module, and several notices carry one. IRM 5.12.2.2 lists 'notices and publications that advise taxpayers that an NFTL may be filed' as Pub 594, CP 501, CP 504, CP 523, Letter 1058, LT-39 and LT-11, and adds that 'the notices sent in the notice stream are sufficient for filing an NFTL'. ACS (IRM 5.19.4.5.3.1): 'Be sure a written warning of NFTL filing is evident on each module ... Examples: CP 501, CP 504 or CP 523 ... an ACS LT11 or LT39'. 'Though no longer a sufficient notice prior to levy, the CP504 and CP523 are valid NFTL warning letters.' IRM 5.12.9.3.1 gives an example: after a CP 501, 'filing of the NFTL for the additional balance due would not be premature'. IRS notice pages: CP501 'we can file a notice of federal tax lien'; CP503 'we may file a Notice of Federal Tax Lien if we haven't already done so'; CP504 'We can also file a Notice of Federal Tax Lien if we haven't already done so'; LT11 'We may also file a Notice of Federal Tax Lien.' In practice, filing waits until the balance reaches a collection unit (ACS or a revenue officer) and the dollar criteria are met.

value.decisionMadeBy: ACS or revenue officer, against the $10,000 guideline

sourceDate: IRM 5.19.4 effective 12-30-2024; IRM 5.12.2 effective 07-12-2024; notice pages last reviewed 16-Dec-2025 (CP503, CP504), 22-Jul-2026 (CP501), 30-Jan-2026 (LT11); accessed 2026-10-11
uncertainty: CP503 says a lien 'may' be filed, but neither IRM list names it as a warning notice. fixedNoticeThatTriggersFiling is null: NOT FOUND, and the IRM ties filing to a determination, not to a notice number. No source says how many days after a given notice ACS typically files.
designImplication: Do not hard-code 'NFTL after CP504'. From CP501 on, the taxpayer is warned. The filing event belongs to the collection-unit stage (after CP504 or LT11) and depends on the balance meeting the $10,000 guideline.

claim: For an individual, state law sets the filing office. IRC 6323(f)(1) and (2): for real property, the office designated by the state where the property is physically located; for personal property, tangible or intangible, the office designated by the state of 'the residence of the taxpayer at the time the notice of lien is filed'. If a state has not designated one office, the NFTL goes to the clerk of the U.S. district court. For D.C. it goes to the Recorder of Deeds. A taxpayer residing outside the U.S. is deemed to reside in D.C. IRM 5.12.7.10, for individuals: 'Real Property - file the NFTL in the recording office for the jurisdiction (usually county) where the real property is located; Personal Property ... in general, file the NFTL at the recording office for the county where the taxpayer resides at the time the NFTL is filed.' Pub 594: 'filed with local or state authorities, such as county recorder of deeds or the Secretary of State offices.' (The Secretary of State is mainly where business personal property is filed.) The IRS deems a mailed NFTL filed on the third business day after mailing, unless state law requires indexing.

value.individualRealProperty: recording office (usually county) where the property is located
value.individualPersonalProperty: recording office (usually county) of taxpayer residence at filing, per state law

sourceDate: IRM 5.12.7 effective 07-18-2025 (5.12.7.10 dated 09-21-2017); IRC 6323 read on Cornell LII; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IRM 5.12.7.10 and its Exhibit 5.12.7-2 (state-by-state filing locations). IRC 6323(f) from https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6323. Pub 594 (Rev. 1-2026).
uncertainty: Exhibit 5.12.7-2 lists each state's office. It was not extracted state by state here. Some states route an individual's personal-property lien to a central state office, not the county.
designImplication: Record the NFTL against the player's county of residence (and the county of any real property). One NFTL can cover several periods (up to 15 statutory liens per IRM 5.12.2.6).

claim: Recording fees are set by each recording office, and the IRS charges them to the taxpayer's account. IRM 5.12.7.12: 'The fees associated with the recording of the NFTL and release need to be charged to the taxpayer's account so that the IRS may be reimbursed when the liability is paid.' IRM 5.12.7.12.3: 'The taxpayer's account is charged up front for both the recording and release fee', posted as TC 360. 'Fee amounts can change over time. Contact CLO for assistance with determining the filing and release fee portions.' Pub 594: the NFTL 'doesn't show your payoff balance or include our charges for filing and releasing the lien'. Pub 1468: 'The taxpayer must also pay all fees that a recording office charges to file and release the lien.' IRM 5.12.3.5.6: when the tax is reduced to zero by adjustment, 'the taxpayer may still be liable for the fee'. Abatement is case by case. 'If all the liabilities on the NFTL are resolved and the filing fee is the remaining balance, ensure the taxpayer is aware of the balance due needed for a lien release.' No IRS-wide dollar amount is published.

value.chargedWhen: up front at filing, for both recording and release
value.amountSetBy: each county or state recording office

establishes: IRM 5.12.7.12 and 5.12.7.12.3. IRM 5.12.3.5.6 (https://www.irs.gov/irm/part5/irm_05-012-003r). Pub 1468 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p1468.pdf), p.3. Pub 594 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p594.pdf), p.5.
uncertainty: amount is null: NOT FOUND. No IRS source publishes a typical or national fee. Amounts vary by recording office and are held in ALS. Any specific dollar figure would have to come from individual county fee schedules, which were not researched. IRM 5.12.7.12.3 says to reverse the TC 360 when an NFTL is filed in error.
designImplication: Add a recording-plus-release fee to the federal balance when the NFTL is filed. Use a modest per-county number from a sourced county schedule, or keep it parameterized and unset until one is sourced. The lien is not released until that fee is paid too.

claim: After an NFTL is filed, the IRS must send Letter 3172 (Notice of Federal Tax Lien Filing and Your Right to a Hearing under IRC 6320) within 5 business days. IRC 6320(a)(2) requires the notice 'not more than 5 business days after the day of the filing of the notice of lien', given in person, left at the dwelling or usual place of business, or sent by certified or registered mail to the last known address. The taxpayer may request a CDP hearing (Form 12153) 'during the 30-day period beginning on the day after the 5-day period' (IRC 6320(a)(3)(B)). IRM 5.12.6.3.6: 'The due date is 30 calendar days after the expiration of the five (5) business days after the date the NFTL is filed (estimated filing date).' The IRS estimates the filing date as the mailing date plus 3 business days. The IRM gives an example: an NFTL mailed Friday Sept 6, 2024 requires the CDP notice to be mailed by Wed Sept 18, 2024. The taxpayer gets 'only one hearing ... with respect to the taxable period'. After that deadline, Form 12153 still allows an Equivalent Hearing for a lien: 'one year plus five business days from the filing date of the Federal Tax Lien', with no court review. Appeals' CDP determination can be taken to the U.S. Tax Court within 30 days. A CDP request suspends the 10-year collection period. Unlike a levy CDP, a lien hearing does not bar levy, though 'normally we will not seize property during these hearings' (Pub 594).

value.equivalentHearingDeadline: 1 year + 5 business days from NFTL filing date

sourceDate: IRM 5.12.6 effective 01-14-2026; Form 12153 (Rev. 7-2022); Pub 594 (Rev. 1-2026); IRC 6320 read on Cornell LII; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IRM 5.12.6.3 and 5.12.6.3.6. IRC 6320(a)(2), (a)(3)(B) and (b)(2) from https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6320. Form 12153 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f12153.pdf), p.3: 'Lien Notice--one year plus five business days from the filing date of the Federal Tax Lien.' Pub 594 p.4-5: 'Within five business days of the first filing of the Notice of Federal Tax Lien for a specific debt, we will send you a Notice of Federal Tax Lien Filing and Your Right to a Collection Due Process Hearing.' IRM 5.12.7.10.5: 'Within five (5) business days, issue the appropriate notice of NFTL filing to the taxpayer (e.g., Letter 3172 ...)'.
uncertainty: The Letter 3172 template was not available as a public PDF (irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/l3172.pdf returned 404). Its wording is taken from IRM 5.12.6, not from the letter itself. Pub 594 says the Equivalent Hearing is 'within one year from the date of the notice', a different anchor from Form 12153's 'one year plus five business days from the filing date'. The two agree in substance, since the notice is due within 5 business days of filing.
designImplication: On NFTL filing, schedule a Letter 3172 within 5 business days and open a 30-day CDP window after it (about 35 to 40 calendar days from filing in total). Allow one lien CDP per tax period and a 1-year Equivalent Hearing fallback. A CDP request pauses the CSED clock.

claim: IRC 6325(a): the IRS 'shall issue a certificate of release of any lien ... not later than 30 days after the day on which' the liability 'has been fully satisfied or has become legally unenforceable', or a qualifying bond is accepted. Release is automatic and the taxpayer does not have to ask. IRM 5.12.3.3: 'Generally, releases are systemically generated through the Automated Lien System (ALS) when all modules on a NFTL are satisfied on Master File.' Pub 1450: 'When all the liabilities shown on the Notice of Federal Tax Lien are satisfied, we will issue a Certificate of Release ... for filing in the same recording office where the notice of lien was filed', and a copy goes to the taxpayer. A written request (Pub 1450, sent to the Collection Advisory Group) is only needed 'If the federal tax lien has not been released within 30 days of satisfying your tax liability'. The 30 days run from satisfaction, including the recording and release fees. When payment is by personal check, 'the 30 calendar day release period begins after fifteen (15) calendar days from receipt'. Payment in guaranteed funds (certified check, cashier's check, money order) at a local office can get an immediate release. Fee: there is no IRS fee to request a release. The recording office's release fee is charged to the account up front at filing (IRM 5.12.7.12.3). A taxpayer who takes a manually prepared Form 668-Z to the recording office pays the recording office's filing fee, and can instead let the IRS file it.

value.from: liability fully satisfied or legally unenforceable, or bond accepted

sourceDate: Pub 1450 (Rev. 7-2018); IRM 5.12.3 effective 09-03-2025; IRC 6325 read on Cornell LII; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Pub 1450 full text. IRM 5.12.3.3 (https://www.irs.gov/irm/part5/irm_05-012-003r). IRC 6325(a) from https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6325. IRS 'Understanding a federal tax lien' page: 'The IRS releases your lien within 30 days after you have paid your tax debt.' Pub 594: release when debt fully paid, bonded, accepted offer's terms met, or 'The period for collection has ended. (In this case, the release is automatic.)'
uncertainty: irsRequestFee: 0 is inferred from the absence of any fee in Pub 1450 and the IRM. No source says 'free' in so many words. The release recording fee amount is NOT FOUND, as for the filing fee.
designImplication: When the federal balance (including lien fees) hits zero, release the NFTL automatically within 30 days, or 45 days if paid by personal check. No player action is needed. A 'request release' action only matters after 30 days have passed.

claim: Withdrawal under IRC 6323(j) removes the NFTL from the public record as if it had never been filed. It does not release the lien or the debt. The IRS 'may withdraw' when: '(A) the filing of such notice was premature or otherwise not in accordance with administrative procedures', '(B) the taxpayer has entered into an agreement under section 6159 to satisfy the tax liability ... by means of installment payments, unless such agreement provides otherwise', '(C) the withdrawal of such notice will facilitate the collection of the tax liability', or '(D) with the consent of the taxpayer or the National Taxpayer Advocate, the withdrawal ... would be in the best interests of the taxpayer ... and the United States.' On written request the IRS must notify credit reporting agencies and named creditors of the withdrawal (6323(j)(2)). The request is on Form 12277 (Rev. 10-2011), which has checkboxes for each ground plus 'The taxpayer is under a Direct Debit Installment Agreement', or any written request with the same information. Withdrawal is discretionary. 'Withdrawal of the NFTL is not mandatory except when the NFTL was filed in violation of the automatic stay in bankruptcy' (IRM 5.12.9.2). A grant is filed as Form 10916(c) in the same recording office. A denial carries Collection Appeals Program rights (Pub 594).

grounds: best interest of taxpayer and US
value.mandatoryException: filed in violation of bankruptcy automatic stay

sourceDate: IRM 5.12.9 effective 09-06-2019; Form 12277 (Rev. 10-2011); IRC 6323 read on Cornell LII; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IRM 5.12.9.2 and 5.12.9.3. IRC 6323(j) from https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6323. Form 12277 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f12277.pdf). Pub 594 p.5: 'A "withdrawal" removes the Notice of Federal Tax Lien from public record ... This doesn't mean that the Federal Tax Lien is released or that you're no longer liable for the amount due.'
uncertainty: No processing time for a Form 12277 decision was found: NOT FOUND. IRM 5.12.9 dates from 2019 and still names 'Streamlined' IAs. A premature-filing request can be decided by the assigned revenue officer. Other grounds go to Advisory.
designImplication: Withdrawal is a separate player action (Form 12277) with a discretionary outcome. It clears the public record but leaves the balance and the statutory lien in place.

claim: Fresh Start (2011) direct debit withdrawal. IRM 5.12.9.3.2.1: 'Generally, an NFTL should be withdrawn if the taxpayer has entered into a DDIA and has met the conditions'. The conditions: 'The aggregate unpaid balance of assessments on the DDIA is $25,000 or less at the time of the request'; the liability 'will be fully paid in 60 months or ... prior to the Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED), whichever comes first'; the request is in writing (Form 12277 preferred); 'The DDIA is active and at least three consecutive electronic payments ... have been processed'; there has been no default on this or any prior DDIA; and no prior withdrawal for the same modules. Qualifying taxpayers are individuals, businesses with income tax only, and out-of-business entities. The IRS page adds: 'If you owe more than $25,000, you may pay down the balance to $25,000 prior to requesting withdrawal'. Taxpayers in other kinds of IA must convert to a DDIA to use this route. 'If a taxpayer defaults on making payment under the DDIA after the NFTL is withdrawn, a new NFTL may be filed.'
sourceDate: IRM 5.12.9 effective 09-06-2019; IRS lien page last reviewed 14-Sep-2026; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: IRM 5.12.9.3.2.1. IRS 'Understanding a federal tax lien' (https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/understanding-a-federal-tax-lien), Withdrawal section. Form 12277 has a checkbox 'The taxpayer is under a Direct Debit Installment Agreement.' Pub 594: 'we routinely grant Notice of Federal Tax Lien withdrawal requests if you've entered into a direct debit payment plan and meet certain other conditions'.
uncertainty: The $25,000 withdrawal threshold is separate from the 2026 $50,000 Simple Payment Plan filing threshold. The IRM states this explicitly ('The criteria for withdrawing an NFTL for a taxpayer in a DDIA is separate and different'). No 2026 source raises the withdrawal threshold.
designImplication: A player with an NFTL who converts to direct debit with balance <= $25,000, pays it off within 60 months and makes 3 consecutive payments can file Form 12277 and expect the public notice removed. Default lets the IRS refile.

claim: Withdrawal after payment in full (Fresh Start). IRM 5.12.9.9: 'There is no legal prohibition on withdrawing an NFTL after the underlying lien has been released.' Under the best-interest ground (6323(j)(1)(D)), it 'will generally be granted if all the following conditions apply: The taxpayer requests the withdrawal in writing; The taxpayer fully satisfied the liabilities on the NFTL; A certificate of release was issued; and The taxpayer is in compliance with filing requirements', meaning all returns for the prior three years are filed and current estimated payments and deposits are made. 'Fully satisfied' includes payment, offset, abatement and full payment of an accepted offer. It does not include expiration of the collection statute, discharge in bankruptcy, or an erroneous release. A self-released NFTL (statute expired) can still be withdrawn under the premature or improper ground, or case by case: two IRM examples grant it after statute expiration. The withdrawal document is Form 10916-A. Form 12277 instructions: 'If you are requesting a withdrawal of a released NFTL, you generally should check the last box regarding the best interest provision.'
establishes: IRM 5.12.9.9 and 5.12.9.9.1. IRS lien page: 'One option may allow withdrawal of your Notice of Federal Tax Lien after the lien's release. General eligibility includes: Your tax liability has been satisfied and your lien has been released; ... You are in compliance for the past three years in filing'. Pub 594: best interest 'could include when your debt has been satisfied and you request a withdrawal.'
uncertainty: The examples of withdrawal after statute expiration are discretionary illustrations, not a rule.
designImplication: After paying off and getting the release, a compliant player (3 years of returns filed) can file Form 12277 and expect the NFTL removed from the public record, as if never filed. A release alone leaves a 'released' NFTL on file.

claim: Several routes exist, with different timing. (1) IRC 6326 administrative appeal for an erroneous NFTL. Per 26 CFR 301.6326-1, as summarized in IRM 5.12.3.9, an NFTL is erroneous if the liability was satisfied before filing, was assessed in violation of deficiency procedures (IRC 6213) or of a bankruptcy stay, or the collection statute had expired before filing. The appeal is available 'within one year after the taxpayer becomes aware of the erroneously filed NFTL'. It may not challenge the underlying deficiency. If the filing is found erroneous, the IRS 'must issue a Certificate of Release within fourteen (14) calendar days', with a statement that the filing was erroneous, which 'assists in repairing the taxpayer's credit or other financial records'. (2) Form 12277 withdrawal under 6323(j)(1)(A) when the filing was 'premature or otherwise not in accordance with the IRS' administrative procedures', for example when an undisputed credit would have paid the balance. The assigned revenue officer can decide it. (3) A CDP hearing (Form 12153) within the 30-day window after Letter 3172, where the taxpayer can check 'I want the Notice of Federal Tax Lien withdrawn' and Appeals decides whether the NFTL stays, is withdrawn or is released. An Equivalent Hearing is available up to 1 year plus 5 business days after filing. (4) The Collection Appeals Program, before or after filing. The fee charged for an erroneous filing is reversed.
establishes: IRM 5.12.3.9 and 5.12.3.9.1. IRM 5.12.9.3.1. Form 12153 lien resolution options ('Withdrawal: ... you believe the NFTL should not have been filed'). Pub 594 p.4-5. IRM 5.12.7.12.3 ('Reverse the TC 360 when an NFTL is filed in error').
uncertainty: 26 CFR 301.6326-1 itself was not read; its content is taken from IRM 5.12.3.9. No processing time for a Form 12277 premature-filing decision was found (NOT FOUND). The 14 days apply 'when practical' ('or as expeditiously as possible').
designImplication: An erroneous NFTL is corrected by release within 14 days of the determination (IRC 6326) or by withdrawal. Either way the fee is reversed. A dispute raised in the CDP window should be the cheapest path for the player.

claim: The lien attaches to all property and rights to property, real or personal, including property acquired after the lien arises. IRC 6321: 'upon all property and rights to property, whether real or personal, belonging to such person.' IRS: 'A lien attaches to all of your assets (such as property, securities, vehicles) and to future assets acquired during the duration of the lien.' Pub 594: 'A lien is a legal claim against all your current and future property ... It applies to property (such as your home and car) and to any current and future rights you have to property (such as wages and bank accounts).' The lien covers tax plus 'any interest, additional amount, addition to tax, or assessable penalty, together with any costs'. The NFTL establishes priority against purchasers, security interest holders, mechanic's lienors and judgment lien creditors (IRC 6323(a)). Before it is filed, those parties can take ahead of the IRS. The IRS adds: 'If you file for bankruptcy, your tax debt, lien, and Notice of Federal Tax Lien may continue after the bankruptcy.'

value.scope: all property and rights to property, real and personal, current and after-acquired
value.nftlPurpose: priority against purchasers, secured creditors, mechanic lienors, judgment creditors

establishes: IRS lien page ('How a lien affects you'). Pub 594 (Rev. 1-2026) p.5. IRM 5.12.1.3-5.12.1.4. IRC 6321 and 6323(a) from Cornell LII.
uncertainty: Exemptions from levy (IRC 6334) do not limit what the lien attaches to. The lien still attaches. Discharge (Pub 783) and subordination (Pub 784) can remove or subordinate it as to specific property. These were not researched in detail.
designImplication: The lien reaches every asset the player owns or later acquires, including car, house, bank balance and wage rights. A filed NFTL is what stops other creditors and buyers from taking ahead of it.

claim: The lien lasts as long as the liability is collectible, which is generally 10 years from assessment (IRC 6502(a): collection 'within 10 years after the assessment of the tax'). The period is suspended by events such as a pending IA or offer, a CDP hearing, bankruptcy plus 6 months, or living abroad for 6 months or more (Pub 594). The NFTL (Form 668(Y)(c)) is self-releasing. It has a 'Last Day for Refiling' column, and 'if the NFTL is not refiled by that date, the lien shall be considered to be released' (IRM 5.12.3.4.1.1). Pub 1468: the date 'is 10 years from the date the liability was assessed plus 30 days'. 'A federal tax lien usually releases automatically 10 years after a tax is assessed if the statutory period for collection has not been extended and the IRS does not extend the effect of the Notice of Federal Tax Lien by refiling it. When a lien is self-released, the Notice of Federal Tax Lien itself is the release document.' 'When the "Last Day for Refiling" passes and no refile has been done, both the statutory lien and the NFTL are immediately released.' 'A certificate of release is not systemically issued for self-releasing liens.' Each period on a multi-period NFTL self-releases on its own date. A refiled NFTL can stay active up to 10 more years, and a refile notice (Form 668-F) is not self-releasing.
sourceDate: Pub 1468 (01-2014); IRM 5.12.3 effective 09-03-2025; Pub 594 (Rev. 1-2026); IRC 6502 read on Cornell LII; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Pub 1468 pp.3-4 and 10. IRM 5.12.3.4.1.1 (https://www.irs.gov/irm/part5/irm_05-012-003r). IRC 6502(a) from https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6502. Pub 594 p.3 lists CSED suspensions.
uncertainty: Pub 1468 is a 2014 publication addressed to recording offices, not taxpayers. Its 10-years-plus-30-days rule matches the IRM. Suspensions of the CSED move the real collection deadline but not the printed refile date, which is why the IRS refiles.
designImplication: Give each assessed period a CSED = assessment + 10 years (plus suspensions) and an NFTL self-release date = assessment + 10 years + 30 days. Unless refiled, the lien and NFTL drop at that date with no release certificate.

claim: The NFTL is a public record. That is its purpose. IRM 5.12.1.4: 'The NFTL is a public notification filed with an office designated by state and local jurisdictions.' Before filing, the IRS 'does not make the lien's existence public until a notice of the lien has been filed' (IRM 5.12.1.2). The IRS's stated effects, quoted as written: IRS lien page, 'Credit — Once the IRS files a Notice of Federal Tax Lien, it may limit your ability to get credit.' CP504 page: 'If the tax lien is in place, you may find it difficult to sell or borrow against your property. The tax lien would affect your ability to get credit ― which may harm your credit rating.' Pub 594: 'Employers, landlords and others may also use this information and not favorably view the fact that a Notice of Federal Tax Lien has been filed against you.' IRM 5.19.4.5.3.1 tells ACS employees to advise the taxpayer of the 'Credit bureau's routine research of public records for this information' and the 'Possibility of poor credit and/or denials of personal loans and credit cards'. A withdrawal removes the NFTL from the public record. A release does not remove it; the release is recorded alongside it. 'After a lien document has been released or otherwise expires, the retention of the document in the public record becomes subject to the archive/purge schedule of the individual recording office' (Pub 1468).

Any claim about credit bureaus' current practice would need a non-IRS source and is not asserted here.
designImplication: Make the NFTL a visible public-record flag that third parties (lenders, landlords, employers) in the sim can consult and may weigh against the player. Do not wire a credit-score formula to it from these sources. Withdrawal clears the flag; release marks it released.

claim: Pub 1 (Your Rights as a Taxpayer) mentions liens only in passing. It says Pub 594 'covers liens, releasing a lien, levies, releasing a levy, seizures and sales, and release of property.' It sets no lien values. The taxpayer rights it lists (to appeal, to a fair and just tax system) are carried out for liens through IRC 6320 CDP, the Collection Appeals Program and IRC 6326, as described in the other entries.
establishes: Pub 1 full text: the only lien-specific line is the cross-reference to Pub 594.
uncertainty: NOT FOUND: Pub 1 contains no NFTL threshold, timing, fee or procedure value.
designImplication: No mechanic comes from Pub 1. Cite Pub 594 and the IRM for lien rules.
